John Sharp's Paradox

ParadoxesSequencesInvariants
Game: Three pieces seem to lose one square when they are rearranged. Find where it went.
How to play: Change the Fibonacci size, then reveal the thin sliver hidden along the joining line.

The square

The rectangle

Look for the math

A 13 by 13 square seems to rearrange into an 8 by 21 rectangle — one square unit shorter. The pieces never change area; the outline lies.

Fibonacci dimensions

Put F(n) for the square's side, F(n−1) and F(n−2) for the cut. The rectangle has sides F(n−1) and F(n+1). Their areas differ by F(n)² − F(n−1)F(n+1) = (−1)ⁿ, Cassini's identity. For n = 7 that is 169 − 168 = 1, the missing square.

The false diagonal

In the square the sloping cut has rise and run 5 and 13; in the rectangle it is disguised as 8 and 8. The slopes differ slightly, so the pieces overlap or leave a thin gap along the join. The logic test computes every piece's area by the shoelace formula for n = 4 through 12: the pieces always conserve area, and the outline is always off by exactly one.

Reveal the sliver, then move the size slider. Does the discrepancy ever change?
